title: What is a memory palace? A duck at the door
description: A memory palace uses familiar places to help you remember a sequence. Try a duck at the door, a lemon on the sofa and one very misplaced umbrella.

cover.alt: A yellow rubber duck sits beside a front door, with a lemon on a sofa visible through the living room doorway
cover.credit: AI-generated realistic illustration created for BrainiLab; a staged example of imagined memory cues, not a research photograph.

practice: Try a few more questions in the General Knowledge Quiz.

sections.title: You already know the floor plan
sections.html:
A memory palace is a familiar place you imagine walking through, with things you want to remember linked to particular stops. It is also called the method of loci.

No chandeliers required. Your flat, a familiar classroom or the route to the kitchen can provide the setting.

sections.title: Why is there a duck at the door?
sections.html:
Suppose your list is duck, lemon, umbrella. Picture a rubber duck blocking your front door, a lemon occupying the sofa and an umbrella sitting in the kitchen sink.

Now mentally follow that route in the same order. Each location gives you a cue for the next item. The scene is imaginary; you can leave the actual sofa alone.

sections.title: Give each stop a job
sections.html:
Stanford’s learning guide recommends a known location, a planned route and memorable images. Choose distinct stops rather than cramming everything beside the door.

This is one kind of mnemonic: a cue that helps you remember. If a long list feels unwieldy, chunking takes a different approach by grouping information.

sections.title: A useful trick, not perfect recall
sections.html:
A 2025 review of adult studies found benefits for recalling items in order, but rated the evidence low to very low in quality.

Treat it as a technique to practise, not a promise of flawless memory. For now, can you retrace your three stops? The umbrella should still be causing trouble in the sink.
